title: Psalm 141: Let My Prayer Rise Like Incense
summary: David asks the LORD to hear him quickly and to receive his prayer like incense and his lifted hands like the evening offering. He asks God to guard his mouth and keep his heart from being drawn toward evil and the company of evildoers, and he welcomes the rebuke of the righteous as a kindness. In the difficult closing verses he looks to God for refuge and asks to be kept from the traps of the wicked.
story: Psalm 141 is the second of four prayers of David for rescue (Psalms 140 to 143) in the Psalter's final Davidic collection. Where Psalm 140 focused on the violence and slander of enemies, Psalm 141 turns inward: the psalmist is concerned not only with what the wicked might do to him but with what they might draw him into. He prays to be kept from evil as well as from evildoers. The psalm shares the language of snares and nets with Psalms 140 and 142, and its closing request to pass by in safety leads into Psalm 142's cry from the cave.
historical:
The heading reads “A Psalm of David.” As with other headings, scholars differ on whether it names the author or marks the psalm's place in a Davidic collection. The psalm gives no specific occasion. Those who connect it with David's life have suggested the years when he fled from Saul, when he had to decide whether to take matters into his own hands (1 Samuel 24 and 26), but the text itself is general.

Verses 5 to 7 are among the most difficult in the Psalter to translate. The Hebrew is compressed and possibly damaged in transmission, and ancient translations and modern versions differ widely in how they render them. The BSB's reading, with rulers thrown down from the cliffs and bones scattered at the mouth of Sheol, is one reasonable reconstruction among several. Readers should hold interpretations of these verses lightly.
cultural:
Verse 2 connects prayer to two regular acts of temple worship. Incense was burned on the golden altar inside the holy place every morning and evening (Exodus 30:7-8), and its fragrant smoke rising toward heaven became a natural picture of prayer rising to God. The evening offering (the Hebrew word minchah often means a grain offering, and is used here for the regular evening sacrifice) was presented daily at the temple along with a lamb (Exodus 29:38-41). The time of the evening offering became a customary hour of prayer: Elijah prayed at that hour on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:36), Ezra at the evening sacrifice (Ezra 9:5), and Daniel at the time of the evening offering (Daniel 9:21). A worshiper far from the temple, or unable to offer sacrifice, could offer prayer and lifted hands in its place.

The delicacies of verse 4 point to the banquets of the powerful, where friendship, alliances, and complicity were sealed over food. To eat at someone's table was to enter into fellowship with them. Oil on the head (verse 5) was a sign of refreshment, honor, and hospitality; guests were anointed with oil at a feast (Psalm 23:5). The psalmist says the rebuke of a righteous man is better than such honors.
literary: Psalm 141 is an individual lament with strong wisdom elements. Verses 1 and 2 are an opening plea for God to hear. Verses 3 and 4 ask God to guard the psalmist's mouth and heart, turning the usual request for protection from enemies into a request for protection from oneself. Verses 5 to 7 contrast the rebuke of the righteous, which the psalmist welcomes, with the fate of wicked rulers, though the text here is obscure. Verses 8 to 10 return to trust and a plea for rescue from traps. The body appears throughout the psalm: hands lifted, mouth and lips guarded, heart kept, head anointed, bones scattered, eyes fixed on God.

outline.t: Guard my mouth and keep my heart
The kindness of rebuke and the fall of the wicked
Eyes on the LORD, kept from the traps

doctrines.note: The psalm treats prayer as an offering to God, parallel to incense and sacrifice. It also shows that prayer is not only for rescue from others but for protection from one's own capacity to sin.
The psalmist asks for guarded speech, a heart kept from evil, and separation from the pleasures of the wicked. Holiness here includes what a person says, what he desires, and whose table he sits at.
Welcoming correction is a mark of wisdom throughout Proverbs. The psalmist calls the rebuke of a righteous man an act of loving devotion and oil for his head, a gift rather than an insult.

words.note: Qetoret, incense. The word refers to the fragrant spices burned on the incense altar in the tabernacle and temple, and to the smoke they produced. Verse 2 asks that prayer be counted as incense before God. The image was taken up in Revelation, where the prayers of the saints rise before God with incense (Revelation 5:8 and 8:3-4).

Minchah, offering. The word can mean a gift or tribute, a grain offering, or, as here, the regular evening sacrifice. Its use in verse 2 connects lifted hands in prayer with the daily worship of the temple. For a worshiper away from the altar, prayer became an offering in its own right.

Yakach, to rebuke or correct. The verb is common in Proverbs, which says that a wise person loves the one who rebukes him (Proverbs 9:8). In verse 5 the psalmist welcomes such correction from the righteous, calling it loving devotion. It takes humility to see a rebuke as kindness.

christ: Psalm 141:2 became one of the church's most used prayers. From early centuries Christians sang it at evening prayer, and it remains central to evening worship in the Eastern Orthodox tradition. Its image of prayer as incense is taken up in Revelation, where the prayers of the saints rise before God with incense (Revelation 8:3-4). The New Testament also teaches that the sacrifices of the temple have been fulfilled in Christ, and that believers now offer a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess his name (Hebrews 13:15). The psalm's longing to have prayer accepted as a sacrifice is met in Christ, through whom believers draw near to God. The prayer for a guarded mouth also echoes in James, who warns that no one can tame the tongue by human effort alone (James 3:8).

hard.q: Why are verses 5 to 7 so hard to understand, and what should a reader do with them?
hard.a: These verses are some of the most obscure in the Psalms. The Hebrew is terse, some words are rare, and the text may have been damaged in copying. Ancient translations such as the Septuagint differ significantly from the traditional Hebrew text, and modern translations disagree about who is being thrown from cliffs, whose bones are scattered, and whose words are pleasant. Some read verse 6 as describing the downfall of wicked rulers, after which the people will recognize that the psalmist's words were true. Others read it as a picture of the psalmist's own suffering community. Verse 7 may describe the bones of the righteous scattered like broken clods of earth, or the fate of the wicked. A careful reader should hold any interpretation of these verses lightly and focus on what is clear in the rest of the psalm: prayer as offering, a guarded mouth and heart, a welcome for correction, and trust in God as refuge. Obscure verses like these remind readers that Scripture was transmitted by hand over many centuries and that translation always involves judgment.

questions: The psalmist prays for protection from his own mouth and heart, not only from enemies. What would it mean for you to pray that prayer?
Verse 5 calls a righteous rebuke an act of loving devotion. When has correction from someone turned out to be a gift to you?
The psalm treats prayer as an offering to God. How might you think differently about prayer if you saw it as something offered rather than only something asked?
